subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the angle between two diagonals of a cube.

mark_split.label: Set the cube on the axes

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.30 — LAQ chapter 3 D.C's & D.R's, answer 19, on a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring Page). Printed appearances: AP 15 · AP 20 · TS 18 · TS 22. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this chapter. It is not a bare guess: the book prints 7-mark splits on three answers elsewhere in the book — LAQ answers 12 (p.24, 1+1+2+1+2), 15 (p.26, 1+1+1+1+1+2) and 21 (p.32, seven 1-mark tags) — so both an even 1-per-move cut and a weighted cut are the book's own shapes at this length. This answer is cut on the moves its own printed working takes, weighted so the two long eliminations carry the most. The book prints a side note here: the angle between the diagonals of a SQUARE is 90°, but for a CUBE it is Cos⁻¹(1/3) — a contrast worth carrying, since the two are easily confused. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The STAR QUESTIONS PLUS bank (pp.104-108) contributes NOTHING to this unit — it holds no D.C's or D.R's question. Paper position: Maths-1B Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say how you would place the cube, and what should happen to the side length.

steps.label: Set the cube on the axes
steps.margin_note: First mark. Nothing in the question fixes a cube, so one is CHOSEN: put a vertex at the origin and three edges along the axes. Every coordinate is then 0 or a, and the side a cancels at the end — so the answer does not depend on the choice.
steps.memory_tip: Nothing fixes a cube, so CHOOSE one: a vertex at the origin, three edges along the axes.
lines: Consider a cube of side 'a' with vertices O, A, B, C, L, M, N, P where O = (0,0,0)
Take A, B, C on the X-axis, Y-axis, Z-axis, then

recall.must_convey: That a cube of side a is placed with one vertex at the origin and three edges along the axes.
accept: put one vertex at the origin and three edges along the axes
take a cube of side a with O at the origin
the three neighbours of O sit on the three axes

choose the cube's position

steps.why: Placing the cube on the axes is a free choice that costs nothing and makes every vertex a triple of 0's and a's. The answer is a pure number, so a must cancel — and it does.
common_mistakes: Trying to answer without choosing coordinates at all.
Placing the cube's CENTRE at the origin, which makes every coordinate a half.

steps.label: Name all eight vertices
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The remaining four vertices follow a pattern: three lie on the coordinate PLANES with one zero each, and the last is (a,a,a) out in space.
steps.memory_tip: Three of the remaining vertices lie on the coordinate PLANES with one zero each; the last is (a, a, a).
lines: Take L, M, N on the XY-plane, YZ-plane, ZX-plane, then
Take P in the XYZ space, then  P = (a,a,a)

recall.must_convey: That the other four vertices are L(a,a,0), M(0,a,a), N(a,0,a) and P(a,a,a).
accept: three more vertices lie on the coordinate planes with one zero each
the last vertex is a comma a comma a

P is the far corner at a a a

steps.why: A cube's vertices are exactly the eight triples built from 0 and a, which is why this labelling is quick once the cube is on the axes.
common_mistakes: Giving a vertex two zeros where it should have one.
Missing the far vertex (a,a,a), which every diagonal needs.

steps.label: Draw the cube
steps.margin_note: Worth no mark but worth drawing. With the cube and its three axes on the page you can read each diagonal's coordinate differences straight off, instead of holding eight vertices in your head.
steps.memory_tip: With the cube drawn you can read each diagonal's coordinate differences off instead of holding eight vertices in mind.

recall.must_convey: That a labelled cube is drawn with the two diagonals OP and CL marked. Naming the drawing is full credit — it cannot be spoken.
accept: draw the cube and mark the two diagonals O P and C L
sketch the labelled cube with its diagonals
make a diagram of the cube showing the two body diagonals
cube geesi rendu diagonals mark cheyyali
draw a labelled cube with the diagonals shown

steps.why: A body diagonal runs from a corner to the corner diagonally opposite THROUGH the cube. The picture is how you check you have taken two of those and not a face diagonal.
common_mistakes: Drawing a face diagonal, which lies in one face and gives a different angle.
Labelling the vertices so that OP and CL turn out to be the same diagonal.

steps.label: Write the two diagonals' d.r's
steps.margin_note: Two marks. A DIAGONAL joins opposite corners through the body of the cube — not a face diagonal. Its direction ratios are the coordinate differences.
steps.memory_tip: A DIAGONAL joins opposite corners through the BODY — not a face diagonal.
lines: d.r's of OP = (a−0, a−0, a−0) = (a, a, a) = (a₁, b₁, c₁)
d.r's of CL = (a−0, a−0, 0−a) = (a, a, −a) = (a₂, b₂, c₂)

recall.must_convey: That the two diagonals OP and CL have direction ratios (a, a, a) and (a, a, −a).
accept: a diagonal joins opposite corners through the body
O P has direction ratios a a a and C L has a a minus a
take the coordinate differences

these are the two body diagonals

steps.why: A cube has four body diagonals; any two of them make the same angle, so picking two particular ones answers the question in general.
common_mistakes: Using a FACE diagonal, which meets an edge rather than crossing the body.
Subtracting the coordinates the wrong way round.

steps.label: Apply the angle formula
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. The a² cancels between numerator and denominator, leaving a pure number — which is why the answer holds for a cube of ANY size.
steps.memory_tip: The a² cancels top and bottom, which is why the answer holds for a cube of any size.
lines: So, angle between the two diagonals is given by

lines.text: ∴ cosθ = 1/3  ⇒  angle between the diagonals of a cube is Cos⁻¹(1/3)

recall.must_convey: That the a² cancels and cosθ = 1/3, so θ = Cos⁻¹(1/3).
accept: apply the angle formula and the a squared cancels leaving one third
cos theta is one over three
the angle is cos inverse one third
a square cancel avuthundi, one by three vasthundi
the answer does not depend on the side

steps.why: The answer being independent of a is the check that the working is right — an angle between diagonals cannot depend on how big the cube is.
common_mistakes: Leaving a in the final answer.
Giving 90°, which is the angle between the diagonals of a SQUARE, not a cube.

insider_note: Put one corner at the origin, not the centre, or every coordinate turns into a half. Choose two body diagonals such as OP and CL, never face diagonals, and the a² cancels to leave Cos⁻¹(1/3) — never 90°.
